path: UCP runs a disciplined suburban campaign; NDP under Nenshi frames the vote as a referendum on Smith; right-flank parties field protest candidates. Derry's affiliation is unclear from the dossier.
Low-turnout campaign; no major scandal breaks; separatist candidate draws protest votes but stays near 10%, shaving the UCP margin modestly.
On September 14 the UCP candidate holds the seat comfortably. Derry wins only if he is that candidate; otherwise he finishes behind.
Brown files for a third term; a councillor challenger launches on housing, encampments and council dysfunction.
Opposition partly consolidates around one challenger; homelessness debates dominate, but Brown leverages name recognition and record.
On November 2 a modest-turnout electorate splits; Brown narrowly holds on, though a single strong challenger keeps it close.
Murdock weighs his record on densification; de Vries positions as fresh pragmatic leadership; slow-growth residents look for their own candidate.
A three-way race forms with incumbent, de Vries and a slow-growth candidate; vote splits along housing lines.
On October 17 the incumbent's base and split opposition favor Murdock or the slow-growth candidate; de Vries is competitive but trails.
Hamer-Jackson runs again on crime and disorder; O'Reilly launches a stability campaign; another councillor or community figure also enters.
Anti-incumbent vote splits between O'Reilly and other establishment candidates; Hamer-Jackson keeps a firm but limited base.
On October 17 voters punish council chaos; O'Reilly is a leading contender, but fragmentation leaves a real chance someone else wins.
Harvie decides whether to seek a third term; if he runs, Achieving for Delta slate lines up behind him with resources.
Fragmented opposition slates attack development and spending but lack a high-profile candidate.
On October 17 Harvie wins comfortably if running; the main downside is a retirement announcement before nominations.
Sulz weighs a third term in a small town facing housing and short-term-rental pressures; a councillor considers running.
If Sulz runs, his incumbency and personal ties dominate; a housing-focused challenger draws newer-resident votes.
On October 17 Sulz wins if on the ballot; substantial risk he retires and an open seat goes to someone else.
Scarpitti signals another run with strong-mayor powers and business backing; challengers are low-profile.
No prominent councillor or ex-MPP enters; campaign is quiet with development and transit themes.
On October 26 Scarpitti wins by a large margin if running; main risk is a retirement decision.
Del Duca runs for a second term on hospital, transit and infrastructure; opponents revive expense and home-property controversies.
A notable challenger gains some consolidation of the anti-Del Duca vote; no new integrity finding lands.
On October 26 incumbency and strong-mayor profile carry Del Duca to a modest win, though the thin 2022 margin keeps upset risk real.
Carter's decision on a third term defines the race; Marimpietri prepares to run, especially if the seat opens.
If open, several councillors enter, splitting votes; Marimpietri's regional profile gives him a base but no lock.
On October 26 Marimpietri wins in some open-seat scenarios; if Carter runs, Carter is favored.
Nuttall seeks a second term on tough-on-disorder record with Conservative networks behind him.
Challengers critique encampment policy and taxes but fail to unify or raise much money.
On October 26 Nuttall wins comfortably in a Conservative-leaning city.
Paterson weighs a fourth term after 12 years; housing and encampment debates dominate Kingston.
If he runs, councillor challengers attack on homelessness; if he retires, an open race draws stronger candidates.
On October 26 Paterson wins if on the ballot; retirement risk is substantial.
McCabe's re-election decision shapes the race; Weber enters as a listed candidate with a local profile.
If the seat opens, councillors also enter; Weber competes in a crowded field on housing and growth.
On October 26 Weber wins only in some open-seat outcomes; otherwise McCabe or another candidate prevails.
Zalepa considers re-election; Wiens prepares a run backed by rural and agricultural support.
Heritage development and short-term rental fights energize voters; a two- or three-way race forms.
On October 26 Wiens is a serious contender, winning strongly if Zalepa steps aside, but trailing a running incumbent more often than not.
Örebropartiet focuses on municipal politics; any Riksdag list is symbolic with tiny resources.
Örebro county voters stick to national parties; the party polls well below 12% in the constituency.
On September 13 it falls far short of both 4% nationally and 12% in Örebro county; no seat.
Trade truce holds at summit level; Commerce and Treasury continue routine designations hitting Chinese entities.
Treasury may hit Chinese refiners over Iranian oil, or Commerce expands a rule; whether it counts as 'new sanctions' is debatable.
By September 30 some qualifying action is plausible but the administration avoids major new measures to protect the truce.
US envoys keep shuttling; Russia insists on Donbas withdrawal; Kyiv refuses to cede unoccupied territory.
Talks produce drafts but no signed ceasefire; fighting continues through autumn.
By October 31 no qualifying signed document with Russia as party; small chance of a trilateral framework signing.
Trump focuses on tariffs, markets and other issues; Buffett stays quiet in retirement.
No major Berkshire announcement prompts a question; Trump's market boasts cite other figures.
September passes with perhaps a stray mention; clear praise of Buffett is possible but unlikely.
PQ leads; CAQ under new leader tries to recover; PLQ rebuilds after leadership turmoil, anchored in Montreal.
Referendum debate pushes some federalists to PLQ; CAQ vote fragments among PQ and PCQ.
On October 5 PQ wins most seats; PLQ's concentrated Montreal vote secures second ahead of a diminished CAQ in most scenarios.
PLQ campaigns as the federalist anchor against a referendum-pledging PQ.
Some strategic consolidation occurs but fragmentation persists; PLQ's ceiling limited outside Montreal and Outaouais.
On October 5 PLQ lands roughly 18-32 seats; 36-39 requires an unusually strong federalist swing.
Vetëvendosje nominates a candidate; opposition and minority MPs threaten to deny quorum and demand consensus.
Rounds fail or are delayed; negotiations over a consensus figure continue, with possible dissolution threats.
By early October either no president is elected or a different consensus candidate emerges; Pula is a long shot.
Russian strikes near Polish and Romanian borders continue; occasional drones stray into NATO airspace.
Allied forces mostly track rather than fire; Poland has authority but shootdowns stay rare.
By September 15 a shootdown is possible if a notable incursion occurs, but the short window favors no qualifying incident.
Droba runs for a third term; Progressive Slovakia decides whether to back him or field its own candidate.
Opposition broadly coalesces around Droba or PS fields a mid-profile rival splitting liberal votes.
On October 24 Droba's incumbency carries a single-round plurality win in most scenarios.
Baška seeks re-election with his regional machine; opposition parties negotiate a joint candidate.
Anti-government mood boosts opposition, but unity is partial and Baška retains strong local networks.
On October 24 Baška wins a plurality in most scenarios given incumbency and low turnout.
Becík runs for a second term with Hlas and coalition backing; opposition and Hungarian parties field candidates.
Hungarian-minority candidate and PS/KDH split the anti-coalition vote; government unpopularity weighs on Becík.
On October 24 Becík narrowly wins on plurality thanks to fragmentation, though a unified opposition could beat him.
Jurinová runs again as centre-right independent; the coalition considers a rival.
Coalition challenger draws rural votes but Jurinová keeps broad cross-party appeal.
On October 24 Jurinová wins a third term in most scenarios.
Trnka seeks a third term; coalition and PS candidates enter.
Fragmented challengers fail to unify; Trnka campaigns on regional record.
On October 24 Trnka wins a plurality in most scenarios.
Vallo runs for a third term with Team Bratislava; challengers are weak or coalition-aligned.
Campaign centers on transport and construction; opposition-leaning capital rallies to the incumbent.
On October 24 Vallo wins comfortably.
PQ leads polls in the low-to-mid 30s; CAQ under new leader seeks a rebound; referendum pledge debated.
Federalists attack the referendum; CAQ and PCQ split francophone non-PQ votes, improving PQ seat efficiency.
On October 5 PQ wins most seats; majority hinges on vote share near 35%, roughly a toss-up leaning short.
CAQ incumbency in Vanier-Les Rivières is weak; PCQ and PQ both target the riding. Paquet's party is unclear.
Three-way race among PCQ, PQ and CAQ in Quebec City suburbs.
On October 5 the winner depends on Quebec City swing; Paquet wins only if he carries the leading party's banner.
Labour selects a candidate to defend Starmer's old seat; Greens and left independents target it. Abdi-Wali's affiliation unclear.
Greens surge in inner London; left vote partly consolidates; by-election date may slip.
By October 9 the result may not even be known; if held, Labour or Green favored, Abdi-Wali an outside chance.
